1. Basic framework for internal controls regarding the financial reporting
   Stephen Hayes Dacus, Representative Director, President & CEO, and Tetsuya Takagi, Executive
   Officer and CFO, are responsible for the design and operation of internal control over financial
   reporting, and have designed and operated internal control over financial reporting in accordance
   with the basic framework for internal control set forth in “On the Revision of the Standards and
   Practice Standards for Management Assessment and Audit concerning Internal Control Over
   Financial Reporting (Council Opinions)” released by the Business Accounting Council.
   Internal control is aimed at achieving its goal to a reasonable extent through basic elements of
   internal control organically intertwining and functioning in an integrated manner. Accordingly, internal
   control over financial reporting may not fully prevent or detect misstatements.

2. Scope of assessment, record date, and assessment procedures
   The assessment of internal control over financial reporting was conducted as of February 28, 2026,
   the last day of the fiscal year, and was performed in accordance with assessment standards for
   internal control over financial reporting generally accepted in Japan.
   In this assessment, we assessed internal control that significantly affects the entire financial
   reporting on a consolidated basis (Company Level Controls), and then, based on the results,
   selected business processes to be assessed. In the assessment of the business processes, we
   assessed the effectiveness of internal control by analyzing the selected business processes, and
   then identifying key controls that have a significant impact on the credibility of financial reporting and
   assessing the design and operation for the key controls.
   During the fiscal year ended February 28, 2026, taking into account the following significant
   changes in the scope of consolidation, we determined the scope of evaluation of internal control
   over financial reporting for the Company, its consolidated subsidiaries, and its equity-method
   affiliates based on the significance of their impact on the credibility of financial reporting.
   ꞏ Seven Bank, Ltd.
        On June 24, 2025, Seven Bank, Ltd. and its consolidated subsidiaries were excluded from the
        scope of consolidation, and Seven Bank, Ltd. became an equity-method affiliate.
   ꞏ K.K. BCJ-95
        On September 1, 2025, 21 subsidiaries under YORK Holdings Co., Ltd., a wholly owned
        subsidiary of the Company, were excluded from the scope of consolidation, and K.K. BCJ-95
        became an equity-method affiliate.
   The significance of the impact on the credibility of financial reporting was determined by considering
   quantitative and qualitative effects as well as the likelihood of occurrence.
   The scope of evaluation of internal controls over business processes was reasonably determined
   based on the results of the evaluation of “Company Level Controls” for the Company and four
   consolidated subsidiaries (five companies in total), three consolidated subsidiaries of K.K. BCJ-95,
   an affiliate of the Company, and Seven Bank, Ltd., as well as the results of the evaluation of
   “Financial Closing and Reporting Processes assessed from an entity-level perspective,” including
   YORK Holdings Co., Ltd., a consolidated subsidiary of K.K. BCJ-95, in addition to the business
   locations described above.
   Business locations determined to have only an insignificant impact on the credibility of financial
   reporting from the standpoint of quantitative and qualitative effects and likelihood of occurrence
   were excluded from the scope of the assessment of Company Level Controls.
   In determining the scope of evaluation of internal controls over business processes, because the
   Group operates multiple businesses, principally convenience store operations under both company-
   operated and franchise formats, as well as leasing and credit card businesses, gross profit from
   operations (after elimination of intercompany transactions) was deemed an appropriate quantitative
   indicator of the relative scale of each business location. Based on this measure, business locations
   were aggregated in descending order of prior-year gross profit from operations (after elimination of
   intercompany transactions), and considering the favorable results of the Company Level Control
   evaluation, two business locations that collectively accounted for approximately two-thirds of
   consolidated gross profit from operations for the previous fiscal year were designated as “Significant
   Business Entities.”
   At the selected Significant Business Entities, sales, accounts receivable, and inventories were
   identified as accounts significantly related to the Company’s business objectives, as they are closely
   related to revenue generation, quantitatively material, and susceptible to material misstatement in
   the Company’s principal business of convenience store operations under both company-operated
   and franchise formats. Accordingly, the business processes relating to those accounts were
   selected for evaluation. Furthermore, despite the designation of certain business locations as
                                                  - 284 -
   Significant Business Entities, we also included other business locations in the scope of evaluation
   and examined accounts involving estimates and forecasts, as well as accounts with a high risk of
   error, in order to assess their impact on financial reporting and identify business processes with a
   high likelihood of material misstatement. Specifically, accounts representing at least 1% of
   consolidated total assets were identified and selected as candidates for evaluation after considering
   their inherent risks and the complexity of the related businesses. Next, significant business
   processes were determined based on their quantitative impact, and the final scope of evaluation
   was established after considering the results of risk assessments and fraud risk analyses for each
   business location. We also reviewed the status of controls over IT systems and considered the
   impact of risks arising from the IT environment when determining the scope of evaluation. As a
   result of these considerations, business processes relating to “tax and deferred tax accounting,”
   “calculation of retirement benefit obligations,” and “valuation of goodwill,” among others, were
   selected for evaluation.

3. Results of the assessment
   As a result of the above assessment, we judged that the Company’s internal control over financial
   reporting was effective as of February 28, 2026.

   None
